title: How often a studio should publish
metaTitle: How often a studio should publish
excerpt: Two or three finished pieces a week beat a hundred thin posts in a day. A new site that publishes everything at once looks automated.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, a few blooms at a time rather than a field dumped all at once.
caption: Poppies against a clear sky, a few at a time and clearly themselves. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How often should a studio publish?
faqs.answer: Two or three finished pieces a week is a strong pace for a studio that still has client work. A hundred thin posts in a day is worse, even if the drafts were ready. Finish the piece, then publish it on a cadence a stranger can believe a person kept.

faqs.question: Should we publish the whole backlog on launch day?
faqs.answer: No. Drafts can be prepared together. Publishing them all on one day makes a new site look automated, and it gives each piece almost no chance to be the one someone reads. Release them steadily, and link each one to pieces already public.

faqs.question: What if we can only manage one piece a month?
faqs.answer: Publish one finished piece a month. A quiet, specific essay is more credible than a weekly post you had to hollow out to hit the calendar. Say what you can sustain, and do not fill the gaps with variations of last month's article.

markdown:
A blog publishing cadence of two or three finished pieces a week beats a hundred thin posts in a day. A new site that publishes everything at once looks automated. Readers can tell, and so can anyone deciding whether to trust the studio behind the site.

The number is not a growth target. It is the rate at which a small team can still mean what it publishes.

## Finished is the unit, not the calendar square

A finished piece answers a question a founder is actually asking. It has a point in the first paragraphs, a structure that teaches the decision, and a link to the next piece or the offer that fits. It has been read aloud, or at least read by someone who did not write it. It does not repeat the previous post with a synonym swapped in.

That standard is incompatible with "we need something live every morning." Mornings are when client work happens. If the blog wins every morning, the practice that gives you something to say will lose. If the blog always loses, you will publish in a panic once a quarter and the site will look abandoned. Two or three finished pieces in a week is a pace that can sit beside project work, if the drafts were started earlier and the editing is real. It is not a pace for inventing the point on the day you hit publish.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the content is produced well or looks hasty, and whether it is mass-produced so that individual pages never get much care. Those questions are the cadence question in different clothes. A schedule that forces hasty pages will fail them. A schedule that lets one person finish a page, and another person say "this is not ready," will pass more often. The guidance also says, plainly, that Google does not have a preferred word count for you to hit. Length is not the cadence. A short page that finishes the decision is better than a long page that repeats itself to look serious. The studio's own range, long enough to finish a decision and short enough not to pad, is an editorial choice. It is not a score.

Count finished pieces. Do not count drafts, ideas, or posts that went live and were corrected for a week because nobody read them first.

## Why a dump looks automated

Preparing many drafts at once is sensible. Publishing them on the same afternoon is not. A new domain that releases a hundred posts in a day looks like a machine turned on. The dates match. The patterns match. The internal links all appear at once, which means none of them were written in response to a page a reader could already open. Even if every draft was careful, the shape of the release says otherwise.

There is a practical cost too. Each post needs a moment as the newest thing: a share, a mention in a conversation, a chance to be fixed if the first reader finds a hole. A dump gives every post the same moment, which is no moment. The best piece in the set is buried under the index. The weak piece gets the same homepage treatment as the strong one, and you cannot bear to unpublish it because "we already announced the library."

Release on a steady cadence instead. Two or three a week is enough for a studio that wants the writing to be part of how people find the work. One a week is enough if that is what "finished" requires. Cluster the release so a new post can link to ones already public. A spoke that points at a hub which is not live yet is a promise to yourself, not a link a stranger can use. Publish the hub first, then the pieces that depend on it.

None of this requires you to pretend the drafts were written on the morning they went out. Say the work was prepared, then edited, then published when it was ready. What you should not do is change dates to look fresh, or add a pile of old pages because you heard that freshness itself is a ranking trick. Google's guidance says that changing dates without a substantial update, and adding or removing large amounts of content just to seem fresh, is a warning sign. Publish when the piece is actually new. Update when the answer actually changed.

## What a small team can sustain

Be honest about who edits. If one person writes between projects, one finished essay a week may be the true ceiling, and two may be a good month rather than a normal week. If the studio reviews together, you can go faster only if review stays real. A cadence that skips review is just a dump spread across the calendar so it looks human.

Protect the time. Put drafting on the same kind of block you would give a client. An essay that is squeezed into Friday afternoon will sound like Friday afternoon. It will hedge, or it will shout, and the founder you wanted will feel both. The pieces that sound like the studio are the ones that were allowed to be specific: a canonical rule, a first screen, a way to brief a project. Those details come from the work. They do not come from a headline generator.

Hanabi's practice is design and engineering, not a newsroom. The public projects, Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, Ballarat Box Sports, Wabisabi, Got Next, Leadly, Trade Moai, are the kind of material worth writing from. A cadence that outruns the work will start borrowing opinions the studio does not hold. That is the moment to slow down. A quiet month with nothing new is cleaner than a month of pieces you would not sign.

Use the client portal and the project notes as a source of questions, not as a source of client secrets. Founders ask the same things. What do we own? What happens to the brand files? What should the homepage say first? Those questions refill the calendar without a keyword tool. If you cannot fill two slots from real questions, you do not have two slots. You have a wish.

## Draft ahead, publish steadily

The useful split is between the backlog and the live site. Keep a list of pieces you are willing to stand behind. Draft them when the thinking is ripe. Publish them on the cadence, after a pass that checks the claim, the links, and the first paragraphs. The backlog can be large. The live site should grow at a human rate.

This split also keeps launch week sane. The marketing site, the domain, and the first projects are enough pressure. Adding a hundred URLs on the same day adds a hundred chances to have the wrong canonical, the wrong share image, and the wrong byline. Ship the site. Then ship the writing as if someone is reading it, because if you are lucky they are.

A simple board is enough. Idea, draft, reviewed, scheduled, published. Do not add a column called "optimize" that means "add the keyword to every heading." The review column should mean a person asked whether the piece is true, whether it repeats a neighbor, and whether the offer it points at is the right one. If it fails, it goes back. A cadence that cannot send work backward is a conveyor.

When you publish, do the small mechanical things in the same gesture. Official URL, description, share image, author, feed item. A piece that is "live" but absent from the feed, or living at two addresses, was not finished. Count it when those are done, not when the markdown was first saved.

## Cadence and the rest of the site

The homepage should not be rewritten to announce every post. A studio site is not a magazine cover. A quiet link to the latest writing, and a blog index that is easy to scan, is enough. The post itself should carry the point. If a piece is important enough to change the homepage, it is probably a change to the offer or the proof, not a blog announcement.

Internal links should appear as the posts appear. The new piece links to older ones that are already true. Next month's piece can link back if the relationship is real. Do not spend the day of publication building a web of links among posts that all went live together and have not been read. You will link out of anxiety. Anxiety links read like a directory.

Keep the voice stable across the cadence. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. A founder as the reader. If week one sounds like a careful studio and week two sounds like a growth blog, you do not have a cadence problem. You have two authors who never agreed, or one author who is tired. Fix that before you add a third post in the week. The archive is a record of how you sound when you think you are being useful. Make it a record you would let a client skim before a call.

Measure the cadence by what shipped and what you would still sign, not by the streak. Skip a slot before you publish a piece you would not send to a buyer. The site will survive.

## When to slow down

Slow down when the pieces start to repeat. Slow down when review is a rubber stamp. Slow down when the questions you are answering are not questions your buyers ask. Slow down before a launch, a rebrand, or a month when the studio is underwater, and say so internally so nobody "catches up" with a dump in the following week.

Speed up only when finished pieces are waiting and the limit is shyness, not quality. Some studios hoard drafts because publishing feels like a claim. Two or three a week is also a cure for hoarding. The claim is smaller when the next piece can correct and extend it. You are not carving a single monument. You are keeping a practice visible.

Do not speed up because a competitor published more. You cannot see how much of their archive they regret. You can see whether your last five pieces are ones you would send to a founder who was about to hire you. If they are, the cadence is working. If they are not, volume will not save them.

## A rate you can say out loud

Tell the truth in planning, even if you never put the number on the site. "We publish two or three finished pieces a week, and we would rather skip than pad." That sentence keeps a content plan from turning into a mill. It also gives you a way to refuse a guest post, a roundup, or a trend piece that does not fit the offer. The slot is scarce on purpose.

The writing still has to live on a site that can hold it. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover that build: a fast marketing site, a real byline, and the engineering to publish steadily without a page-builder mess.

A pace is not a result. [Measuring a studio blog by conversations](/blog/measuring-a-studio-blog-by-conversations) is the next piece, because two or three posts a week only matter if the right buyer sometimes writes back.
